extracted.intended_audience: legislators, educators, and readers of political/philosophical treatises on civic education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines from Aristotle on which kinds of music, harmony, rhythm and instruments should be taught as part of civic education, how instruction should be age‑regulated, and how music relates to moral formation and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music must not impede civic duties or render the body effeminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning music should never prevent the business of riper years, nor render the body effeminate and unfit for the business of war or the state; it should be practised by the young and judged of by the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music training must be balanced against practical civic and military obligations. Instruction should not undermine physical fitness or public responsibilities; elders should assess what musical instruction is appropriate for future citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriate instruction—avoid disputed and virtuoso pieces for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should not be employed in those parts of music which are the objects of dispute between the masters in that science; nor should they perform such pieces as are wondered at from the difficulty of their execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children only so much as enables them to receive proper pleasure from excellent music and rhythms — more than the mere animal/instinctive feeling, but not technical virtuosity. Reserve technical, contested, or showy repertoire (public-prize pieces) for advanced students or specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection—prefer simple, morally suitable instruments for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should never be taught to play upon the flute, or any other instrument which requires great skill, as the harp or the like, but on such as will make them good judges of music or any other instruction; the flute is not a moral instrument but one that will inflame the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose instruments for learners that develop musical judgement and moral disposition rather than technical display or passion. Instruments that demand great skill or are linked with passionate/ritual uses (e.g., flute) are inappropriate for freemen's youth; confine them to professional performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist professionalization of freemen—virtuosity should be for professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not teach freemen to play like masters (virtuosos); such practice is unfit for freemen and should be confined to those who are paid for doing it, because it usually gives people sordid notions and makes artists regulate their bodies to please spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid training citizens as entertainers who adjust art to the whims of audiences; professional performance and its moral risks (dependency on spectators, sordid aims) should be separated from civic education. Virtuoso training is legitimate for paid specialists or contestants for artistic prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match harmony/rhythm to educational purpose (moral vs. entertainment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody is divided into moral, practical, and enthusiastic kinds; each corresponds to particular harmonies. Music should be applied to many purposes but the most moral harmonies should be used in education; enthusiastic harmonies for pleasing audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select harmonies according to intended effect: use ethical (moral) melody/harmony for character formation, practical melodies for instruction, and enthusiastic (pathetic) forms for excitement or spectacle. Do not use the same music for all ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Doric (ethical) harmony for civic education; Phrygian and others for specific effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In education ethic melody and ethic harmony should be used, which is the Doric. Phrygian is pathetic and raises the mind (suitable for bacchanal/violent emotions), while Doric is serious and fittest to inspire courage; Lydian may be elegant and instructive for a child's age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Doric harmony as the default for teaching that aims at seriousness and courage. Recognize Phrygian's power to inflame and Lydian's gentleness; allocate harmonies by the moral/affective effect desired and by the learner's age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use music therapeutically—to purify and soothe passions
rubrics_metrics.description: All music which has the power of purifying the soul affords a harmless pleasure; sacred music can soothe minds rendered enthusiastic and restore tranquillity with pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include forms of music that calm and 'purify' strong passions in educational and therapeutic contexts. Employ sacred or sedative music to restore composure for the compassionate, fearful, or passionate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust music to age and natural capacity—observe moderation, possibility, and decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three boundaries of education: moderation, possibility, and decorum. What is possible and what is proper must be considered; for instance older people cannot sing very high notes and should employ gentler harmonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select repertoire and style that are feasible for learners' physical and developmental stage (possibility), that are moderate (avoid extremes), and that fit social/ethical norms (decorum). Tailor musical choices across life stages accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre and public performance music must suit a mixed audience and aim at universal pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who contend upon the theatre should exhibit harmonies that are moral and according to nature so as to give pleasure to everyone, because audiences are composed of free and instructed, rude mechanics, hired servants, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public spectacle, prefer species of music that appeal widely and accord with human nature rather than pandering to the perverted tastes of particular social groups. Differentiate between music for education and music for public entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject instruments/practices that impede speech or civic interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute prevents the player from speaking, and for that reason it was forbidden to youth and freemen by forefathers; some instruments were discarded because they contributed nothing to the improvement of the mind or were otherwise harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disallow musical practices that physically or socially impede the citizen's other capacities (e.g., rhetorical speech) or do not contribute to moral/intellectual improvement.
